content.title: Ohio State spring football takeaways: Julian Sayin grows, Tavien St. Clair shines
content.text: COLUMBUS, Ohio — In a rainy Ohio Stadium, the Ohio State Buckeyes debuted a new-look team to the 40,240 fans in attendance.Though receiver Jeremiah Smith and quarterback Julian Sayin are back as returning stars, 51 new players saw their first playing time in front of fans.The defense won 35-26, a flip from the offense’s dominance a year ago. Sayin ran for one touchdown and threw one interception on a tipped pass, while backup Tavien St. Clair had a promising performance, throwing for one touchdown.It was a mixed bag for both sides of the ball, though, but there were enough bright spots from the limited starter snaps and the backups to bring some encouragement, and maybe some concern, going into the summer.Here are thoughts from the game:Sayin runs it in for a touchdownSayin didn’t come into Saturday’s game with a lot to prove regarding his arm. He completed 77 percent of his passes a year ago and showed a complete ability to make every throw on the field.Sayin completed 8 of 15 passes for 82 yards, one interception and 10 yards on two rushing attempts. He needed to show progress with his legs, even if the defense couldn’t hit him, and he did that right away.Sayin’s first drive was hampered by poor play from the offensive line, which played without both starting tackles, but it still resulted in a 6-yard fourth-down touchdown run. That run would’ve produced a big hit in a live game, as he ran into the corner of the end zone while being chased by transfer linebacker Christian Alliegro.Sayin, though, said he would’ve lowered his shoulder if this was the regular season or playoffs.“I’m 100 percent scoring,” he said. “You know, as a quarterback, there’s going to be moments where you have to drop your shoulders and go get the first down or go get a touchdown for the team.”Hearing that from Sayin alone shows some growth. There’s a different level of confidence coming from Sayin’s voice this year. He’s not the first-year quarterback who was trying to win the starting job. Now, he’s a second-year quarterback who is trying to be more than just a general on the field. He knows he needs to be a playmaker for the Buckeyes.He did that on his second drive as well, scrambling for a first down.Ohio State coach Ryan Day said it’s hard to judge Sayin’s growth in a spring game, but Sayin has put in the time to make it a priority through 15 practices.“It’s been an emphasis point, and you can see that he’s aware of that,” Day said. “He was moving well this spring, but certainly it’s a lot different when you’re live, and so that’s going to be the challenge to continue to work on, pocket presence and then making plays with his legs.”We’ll see how that translates when preseason camp begins in August and into the season, but that was a good showing from Sayin, even if he didn’t throw a touchdown pass. He didn’t need to light the world on fire to leave the field happy about his performance; the California native just had to show growth.Backup quarterback Tavien St. Clair (9) stole the show during Ohio State’s 2026 spring football game.Ben Jackson / Getty ImagesSt. Clair is a different player than a year agoSpeaking of growth, nobody on offense showed more than St. Clair on Saturday.The second-year quarterback was the No. 7 player in the 2025 class and the No. 3 quarterback, so he arrived in Columbus with high expectations, but fans knew it would take time with Sayin taking over the starting role.St. Clair struggled mightily in his first spring game, throwing two interceptions and looking a bit out of sorts from the speed of the game. He even struggled in the practice before Saturday’s spring game, although some of those mistakes might’ve been from being overly aggressive.On Saturday, he looked perfectly in rhythm. St. Clair completed 9 of 21 passes for 166 yards and one touchdown. He looked locked in from the start, throwing a deep sideline ball to five-star freshman receiver Chris Henry. He followed that up on the next drive with a 40-yard touchdown pass to Henry.“I think you can see the talent for sure,” Day said. “He threw some really nice balls down the field and then, you know, missed as well. And some of the drives got stymied, but that’s part of it. He has to learn from those things and continue to grow.”St. Clair had strong moments, showing off his arm strength and even made some tight window throws. The Bellefontaine, Ohio, native has always passed the eye test from a physical perspective. He’s 6-foot-4 and 230 pounds and can move out of the pocket, both rolling out to run and to throw, which he displayed Saturday.The biggest thing, though, was him mixing athleticism with arm talent and showing that he can be the quarterback of the future if he continues to progress.Henry shines in first Ohio State lookOhio State’s receivers had a good day overall, but none, with the exception of Smith, had more offseason hype than Henry.The five-star caused a lot of sleepless hours for the coaching staff during Big Ten championship week as they tried to lock down his recruitment. They ultimately did, and he showed why he was so highly touted on Saturday. He was St. Clair’s favorite target when he was in the game and was much more than a deep threat. He caught a few routes in traffic and dropped one pass while falling down, in addition to two receptions beyond 30 yards. Henry finished with four catches for 96 yards.Ohio State’s receivers had a fairly good day. Smith didn’t play past the first drive, transfer Devin McCuin made a couple contested catches and Brandon Inniss didn’t play much, either.But Henry’s performance is going to put new receivers coach Cortez Hankton in a tight position, trying to find out where to play Henry in a deep receiver room.Backup offensive line struggles, Ian Moore looked fineThe offensive line struggled, as expected.The Buckeyes were down both Austin Siereveld and Philip Daniels, along with Josh Padilla. Their absences forced second-year lineman Carter Lowe to play tackle one-on-one against Kenyatta Jackson. He struggled against Jackson, who is arguably Ohio State’s best pass rusher. Lowe, a four-star prospect from Toledo, was put in a tough situation and should learn from that performance. It’s still too early to judge him on that, but Ian Moore, on the left side, has been at Ohio State a year longer and may be stepping into a starting role next year, with a good offseason.He started at left tackle, and while he struggled at times, he was less noticeable than Lowe, which is a good sign for his future chances of working into the rotation.There’s still room to grow for Moore, but if he can put together a strong offseason, he can be included in Ohio State’s plans for next year.Devin Sanchez is going to be a starSayin’s second throw of the game was a back-shoulder throw to Smith, on the near sideline. It was a well-placed throw, but it had no chance of being caught because of how well Sanchez defended the ball.Excuse my hyperbole here, but there’s a real chance that Sanchez turns into an All-American corner before his time is up at Ohio State. That’s not just because he won that one rep, but also everything he’s done since the end of last season.Despite the loss to Miami, I thought Sanchez played a good game and even had a pass breakup. Since then, though, he’s only elevated. While practice hasn’t been open to the media all spring, between the practices we’ve seen, especially the Friday before the spring game, and the clips posted on social media, it’s been evident that Sanchez has stepped into the five-star hype many placed on him as a freshman.That’s not to say he won’t get beat at times next season, but if Ohio State was going to have another elite defense, it had to develop at corner after losing Davison Igbinosun and Lorenzo Styles. A lot of that fell on Sanchez.So far he looks like he’s done just that and elevated his game. His offseason isn’t over. He still has to build on this spring in preseason camp and remain healthy, but the combination of Sanchez, Jermaine Mathews Jr. and Georgia transfer Dominick Kelly, mixed with the safeties, could be a lethal group for the Buckeyes. It won’t get the hype as the best secondary in the country — there’s still a lot of in-game unknowns there — but it’s a unit that is deep and has an extremely high ceiling as it grows together.
